inline.s: The essential point of observing the mind is this: watch the present thought. When a deluded thought arises, look at it closely and it vanishes; a moment later it arises again, and again you look closely and again it vanishes; if no deluded thought arises, simply keep watching. Continue in this way until, after long and thorough practice, you see that not a single thought arises — then you are in accord with prajñā. At that time there is observation without thought, and no-thought while observing. The Awakening of Faith says: “If one can observe no-thought, one is thereby tending toward the Buddha’s wisdom.” The state of no-thought is excellent, and it is deep, vast, and inexhaustible; but do not pursue it or cling to it. When thoughts are present, know them and do not follow them; when no thoughts are present, still maintain awareness — still and yet illumining, illumining and yet still. As it is said, “With thoughts, observe the thought; without thoughts, observe emptiness.” Look toward the place from which a thought arises; if a thought arises, you must see it at once. If you practice the work of observing the mind ever more deeply, then subduing afflictions, removing habitual tendencies, and freeing yourself from sorrow and suffering — attaining single-minded concentration — is a natural and spontaneous matter. Patriarch Bodhidharma said: “The single Dharma of observing the mind encompasses all dharmas; it is the most essential and concise.” (Treatise on Breaking the Marks)

One should constantly observe (be aware of) one’s thoughts; this is extremely beneficial and also interesting. Generally speaking, there are three situations. First, the observation is focused and continuous — then there is only right mindfulness (the mindfulness that is awareness) and no deluded thought. Second, the observation is not continuous, so right mindfulness and deluded thoughts alternate. In that case, carefully observe the logical relation between the preceding thought and the following one; this is not only interesting, it also helps you understand this so-called “self” better, and it helps you make the transition to the first situation. Third, observation is lost and one falls entirely into deluded thinking — there are only deluded thoughts and no right mindfulness. The first situation is the one we aim to reach; the second must be carried on under supervision; the third must be entirely eliminated.

Awareness of thoughts is a sharp weapon for stilling delusion, removing attachment, and breaking through confusion; the ancients likened it to a mirror that reveals demons. In the same way, this practice must be done not only on the cushion but also a great deal off the cushion: while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; with eyes open and with eyes closed; seizing every spare moment to practice — practice! practice! practice! Form the habit of observing the mind at all times and in all places, until habit becomes second nature.
Question: When observing the mind, I cannot see any thoughts. What should I do?

Answer: At the beginning this happens; there is no need to worry. It is enough simply to know that you are observing the mind attentively. If your attention is lost, gather it back at once — lose it and immediately recover it. You must cultivate the ability and the habit of observing the mind attentively, continuously, and persistently. Going further, you must attain this: when a deluded thought arises, know it and do not follow it.
Question: When observing the mind, from where should the observation begin?

Answer: On this point, Mr. Nan Huaijin said: “The pure prajñā method of observing the mind contemplates the arising and perishing of one’s own mind, intellect, and consciousness; originally there is no question of where the observation should begin — that is fussing like an old woman, a needless complication! The mind is not within, without, or in between. Yet when ordinary practitioners do this contemplation, they easily concentrate their attention in the head, which brings on high blood pressure and other ailments; therefore a skillful means was offered for everyone to contemplate gently at the heart. And lest you not understand what is meant by the heart, it is specially explained as the pit of the stomach, the place between the two nipples, the hollow where the ribs meet (
commonly called the yellow court, the heart cakra, the heart’s place, which is also the location of the shanzhong acupoint
). It is right here that one naturally begins the contemplation.” (A Preliminary Study of Samādhi and Prajñā))
Question: Sometimes deluded thoughts circle around and will not leave. What should I do?

Answer: Simply calm your mind and, in fine detail, look back at that thinker; observe it without any judgment and see what it wants to think about. When you observe in this way, the power of the deluded thought swiftly weakens and finally ceases. A while later it arises again, and again you observe in the same way, until it ceases. This is “observing the thought, and the thought at once abides (ceases)” — a good method for stilling deluded thoughts. Once you have gotten the knack of gathering in the mind and of observing delusion, some creative methods will surface of themselves; then take up the cycle of “apply, review, improve (draw up a new plan); apply again, review again, improve again (draw up a new plan),” going deeper and deeper. In time you will form a complete set of methods for all hours of the day.

One should often, with curiosity and keen interest, carefully look back at what that thinker is thinking, and manage to know it without following it. In this way you are both stilling delusion and cultivating the power of awareness — two gains in one act. Throughout the whole course of studying Awareness Chan, a focused, continuous, and lasting power of awareness is of the utmost importance; when the power of awareness is strong, everything else is easy. So seize every time and opportunity you can to strengthen your awareness — this is the most basic and most effective method.
Question: Who is it that looks back at that thinker?

Answer: It is the master within who observes. When deluded, the thinker is in charge; when awake, the master within is in charge. The heart of the path of liberation is that the master within should be in charge.
Question: What does “observe the thought, and the thought at once abides; be aware of delusion, and delusion is all true” mean?

Answer: This is a passage of Chan practice recounted by Master Tanxu in his autobiography, Recollections of Shadows and Dust: “When I first sat, deluded thoughts arose without cease, like waves in the sea, one wave chasing the next and the next chasing the one after, never stopping; I could not suppress them, and I grew very anxious. Later I stopped suppressing them and instead used the power of contemplation to observe them, watching from where on earth the deluded thoughts arose. Observed in this way, the deluded thoughts vanished; having vanished, they arose again, and when they arose I observed again. After a long time, the deluded thoughts gradually ceased to arise, and my mind became very peaceful and natural.”

One evening, during the second late incense sitting, I felt that I had barely crossed my legs when the signal to end the sitting sounded; later a neighbor on the next mat told me that a full long incense stick had long since burned through. During that one sitting, though it seemed no great time had passed, I felt my body and mind utterly at ease and wholly in accord with the Dharma, with an indescribable sense of benefit, and imperceptibly, from the ground of my nature, two lines welled up: ‘Observe the thought, and the thought at once abides; be aware of delusion, and delusion is all true.’ At first I did not dare to consider these two lines correct; later I went and asked old Master Di (Master Dixian), and old Master Di gave them his seal of approval.”

Observe the thought, and the thought at once abides” means: when deluded thoughts arise without cease, observe them attentively and they stop. “Be aware of delusion, and delusion is all true” means: the deluded mind and the true mind are two states of the mind; when you illumine with awareness this mind of deluded thought (the deluded mind), it transforms into the thought-free true mind.

Master Tanxu said: “Therefore, when one first applies effort, do not fear that there are deluded thoughts. When deluded thoughts are present, use the wisdom that can observe to observe them, and the deluded thought at once abides (the deluded thought stops); at the same time, be aware and illumine that this deluded mind is itself the true mind — there is no true mind apart from the deluded mind.”

blocks.text: 3. Not Apart from the Present Thought

inline.s: Not apart from the present thought means that whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one is never apart from awareness of the present thought, and one attains “the thought arises, and one is aware at once” (as soon as a deluded thought arises, one sees it immediately). If a deluded thought arises, at once cry out a rebuke (for example: Wrong!), cut it off, and do not let it continue; if no deluded thought arises, simply keep watching. Alternatively, if a deluded thought arises, with a stern alertness be aware of it, and being aware of it, it is gone. Or again, if a deluded thought arises, watch what it wants to think about, and the deluded thought ceases of itself. In short, there are many particular methods for cutting off deluded thought; each person should use the one suited to his or her own situation. But one must without fail attain “the thought arises, and one is aware at once; being aware of it, it is gone,” until not a single thought arises.

The practice of not being apart from the present thought is extremely important; it is the basic skill of Chan investigation. Therefore practice it on the cushion, and practice it off the cushion; practice while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down; practice throughout all the hours of the day, practicing until it is firmly and solidly established.

The study and practice of this stage is in fact the continuation and deepening of “know it and do not follow it” from the preceding section. From “know it and do not follow it” one must go further and attain “the thought arises, and one is aware at once; being aware of it, it is gone,” until not a single thought arises and movement and stillness become one piece.

At this stage, if awareness is focused and continuous, deluded thoughts do not arise; with the slightest lapse, deluded thoughts arise at once. Therefore one must always maintain awareness and work at “the thought arises, and one is aware at once”: as soon as a deluded thought arises, be aware of it immediately and do not let it continue. At all times check whether you have fallen into the world of the head (into deluded thinking); if you have, that means awareness has been lost, and you must raise it up at once. Once awareness is raised, it is like the sun high in the sky: the sprites and specters hide away, deluded thoughts leave no trace or shadow, and the hard ice of habitual tendencies begins to melt. Having reached this point, one should place one’s attention on not losing awareness. When this is long and thoroughly matured, one enters the realm where not a single thought arises.

The practice of not being apart from the present thought must be carried out in two aspects: one is to strengthen one’s own power of awareness, and the other is to weaken the power of sense-objects to entangle one. The work of weakening the entangling power of sense-objects is done in the midst of daily arising of mind and stirring of thoughts, through seeing through and letting go. The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Knowing the illusion, one is at once free of it, without resort to skillful means; being free of the illusion, one is at once enlightened — there are no gradual stages.” The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: “One is able to distinguish well all the marks of dharmas, yet in the ultimate truth one does not move.” (One can clearly discern all dharmas, yet the mind is not moved by these illusions.) On this subject, in the “College of Online Buddhist Studies, Practice According to the Teaching,” the
Chan School

stage materials on “prajñā breaking through delusion” (A Detailed Explanation of the Diamond Sūtra, A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sūtra, A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, and Selected Annotations on the Sūtra of the Treasury of Buddhas) all discuss this in detail. Always observe: what is it that pulls you away from the present moment and plunges you into deluded thinking? You must find out the events and causes that pull you away from the present, and prescribe the right remedy, treating the most serious first. Especially at critical moments, you must be able to forbear, and then be able to transform.

[Ultimate truth: the supreme principle, that is, the true reality of all dharmas. The Buddha said: “All dharmas are false; where they cease, that is called the real, is called true reality, is called the dharma realm, is named ultimate wisdom, is named the ultimate truth, is named ultimate emptiness.” (Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra
Chapter Forty
Kaundinya Chapter)

Not being apart from the present thought is the foundation for breaking through the three barriers. Let awareness of the present thought be unbroken, maintain no-thought (not a single thought arising), let movement and stillness become one piece, and then, within no-thought, look into and behold your original face. Master Hanshan said: “The tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used were meant only to have you use the huatou to block the flow of deluded thoughts from the faculty of mind so that they cannot proceed, and right at the place where they cannot proceed, to look into and behold your original face.” (Collected Works of Dream Wanderings
Essential Instructions on Chan Investigation)

Master Hanshan also said: “As things stand now, within the dream of ignorance, how can old karma be dissolved? One must use the light of wisdom to shine through and break ignorance, and truly believe that one’s own mind is originally pure, and not be driven by deluded and inverted thoughts; then all karma is without cause, because (since) deluded thought is the cause of all karma. Why is this so? From beginningless time we have been deluded about our own original mind, and life after life we have created all kinds of karma with the mind of deluded thought. The habitual seeds of karma accumulate within the eighth consciousness (the ālaya consciousness), and are watered by the water of ignorance, causing these evil seeds to send forth (produce) the sprouts of karma — this is the root of sin, and all evil karma arises from it. Now, wishing to dissolve old karma, one must first arouse the great light of wisdom, shine through and break ignorance, and not permit deluded thoughts to sprout and grow stealthily in the dark. If one can cut off a deluded thought at the very place where it arises, then the accumulated root of old karma is dissolved on the spot. As it is said, ‘Fear not the arising of a thought; fear only that awareness comes too late.’ If awareness and illumination are slightly late, one is turned around by it. If one can, in the midst of daily arising of mind and stirring of thoughts, be aware of and extinguish each thought as it comes, this is what is meant by ‘All sins are like frost and dew; the sun of wisdom can dissolve them.’ For the darkness of ignorance can be broken only by wisdom — this is what is meant by ‘wisdom can dissolve them.’ If you do not let go of it day or night, diligently observing, and do not let it pass, but at the very place where deluded thought arises, investigate it to the end and find no mark of arising — look and look again, and in the end it cannot be found. When this is long and thoroughly matured, your own mind is pure and without a thing, and the mind without things is true reality. If you constantly observe this mind, what deluded thought can abide in it, what accumulated karma can lodge there? … One must take awareness and illumination as the foundation of practice. … Without the light of wisdom, how can one break the darkness of delusion? Only be sure that awareness and illumination are not obscured and the light of wisdom appears — that is the time to finish with karmic hindrances and emerge from birth and death.” (Collected Works of Dream Wanderings
Showing Dong Zhiguang)

Master Hanshan also said: “What is called cultivation is simply following along with one’s own mind and purifying away the shadows of deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies (deluded thoughts and habitual tendencies are both illusory and unreal, and so they are called shadows). To apply effort here is what is called cultivation. If a single thought of delusion suddenly ceases, and one sees thoroughly that one’s own mind is originally perfect, luminous, vast, pure by nature, and utterly without a thing, this is called awakening. … In doing the work nowadays, one must first cut away (the same as ‘shovel away’) intellectual understanding, and work precisely and solely on the single thought. Truly believe that your own mind is originally perfectly clean, not hanging by a single thread, round and bright, filling the dharma realm. Originally there is no body, mind, or world, and no deluded thoughts or emotional cares. This very single thought is itself unborn. All the various states now before you are illusory and unreal; they are only shadows appearing within the true mind. Having seen through them in this way, then at the place where deluded thoughts arise and cease, fix your gaze steadily upon them. Watch them: from where do they arise, and to where do they cease? Press hard upon them in this way, and whatever deluded thought it may be, one press shatters it to bits; on the spot it melts like ice and crumbles like tiles. Never follow along with it, and never let it continue — this is what Yongjia meant by ‘one must cut off the mind of continuity.’ For the false and floating mind has originally no root or thread; never take it as a real thing and let it lie across your chest. When it arises, simply shout (
duō

, a scolding cry), and with one shout it vanishes. Never suppress it (never press the thought down), for then it will do as it pleases with you (otherwise you will be turned around by it), like a gourd on the water (press this one down and that one floats up). Simply cast body, mind, and world to one side and single-mindedly raise this one thought. Like a precious sword sweeping across the sky, be it Buddha or Māra, it cuts all off at once, like cutting through tangled silk. Press on with naked, bare strength — this is what is meant by ‘the straightforward mind is the right mindfulness of true suchness.’ Right mindfulness is no-thought. To be able to observe no-thought may be called tending toward the Buddha’s wisdom.” (Collected Works of Dream Wanderings
Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan)
Had Liu Yi not carried the letter, by what cause would he ever have entered Lake Dongting?
The method of Chan investigation was brought to our land by the First Patriarch, Bodhidharma. The Patriarch transmitted to the Second Patriarch, Huike, the method of Chan investigation, saying:
“Externally, put an end to all conditions; internally, let the mind have no gasping; with the mind like a wall, one may enter the Way.”
(See
A Detailed Explanation of the Treatise on the Two Entrances and Four Practices
) As for the Sixth Patriarch, he taught people:
“Not thinking of good, not thinking of evil, at precisely such a moment
(at this very moment)
, what is the original face of the Venerable Ming
(what is your original face)

?” “If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, simply do not think about anything good or evil, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-substance, serene and ever still, with wondrous function as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
(See
A Detailed Explanation of the Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch

) Later, because people’s faculties had become coarse and inferior, to directly require them to put an end to all conditions externally and not think of anything good or evil was in fact impossible. Hence the appearance of koan Chan, which taught people to investigate a koan, and by that means to remove discriminating consciousness as they practiced Chan. By the time of Chan Master Dahui, koan Chan had developed into huatou Chan, which he vigorously advocated, making it the mainstream of the Chan school.

The process of Chan investigation is: the ten thousand thoughts return to one, the one returns to nothing; investigate earnestly and see through to the original nature (understand the mind and see the nature); cut off all view-afflictions and thought-afflictions, thereby ending segmental birth and death; then further, end transformational birth and death and perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. Master Hanshan said:

“When the ancients investigated and sought, they sought the truth and the ultimate only at the crossroads of birth and death; they did not, apart from this, treat the ink and paper writings and the twelve divisions of the Three Vehicles’ teachings as something extraordinary.”
(Collected Works of Dream Wanderings·Showing the Seat-Master Miaozhan)

[Segmental birth and death: for sentient beings within the three realms and six paths, because of the karma of good and evil deeds they have done, their lifespan has a limit and their bodily form has divisions; hence their birth and death is called ‘segmental birth and death.’ One who ends segmental birth and death escapes rebirth and leaves the three realms. Transformational birth and death: for the sages among the Three Vehicles who have already cut off the delusions of views and thoughts and have ended segmental birth and death — in the course of cultivating the path, deluded thinking gradually ceases and realization gradually increases; this shifting of delusion and enlightenment differs in each period, and the passage from the former period into the latter is just like one round of birth and death, hence it is called ‘transformational birth and death.’ One who ends transformational birth and death perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. Duande: the ins and outs, the root cause, the ultimate. The twelve teachings:

refers to all the scriptures and teachings. The content of the scriptures and teachings is altogether divided into twelve categories, so it is called the twelve divisions of the teachings, also known as the twelve divisions of the sutras.

blocks.text: Holding Up a Flower and Smiling

inline.s: Question: What is the meaning of “holding up a flower and smiling”?

Answer: “Holding up a flower and smiling” means that the World-Honored One held up a flower and Kāśyapa smiled. It is also rendered “holding up a flower, a single smile”; this is the first koan of the Chan school’s mind-to-mind transmission.
The Compendium of the Five Lamps
Chapter on the World-Honored One says:
“When the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he held up a flower and showed it to the assembly. At that time the humans and gods numbered a million, and all were at a loss
(they did not know what to do)
, and only the golden-skinned ascetic
(Mahākāśyapa)

broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: I have the treasury of the correct Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the subtle Dharma gate of true reality without marks, not established on words, a special transmission outside the teachings — I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa
(that is, Mahākāśyapa)
This event is recorded in the Sūtra of the Great Brahmā King’s Questions to the Buddha on Resolving Doubts
Chapter Two: Holding Up a Flower
, where the sutra says:

“At that time, the lord of the Sahā world, the Great Brahmā King named Fangguang, took the wonderful Dharma-lotus golden-light great utpala flower, the root of the accomplishment of the three-thousand-great-thousandfold world, and holding it up, offered it to the Buddha; then he withdrew, paid homage, and said to the Buddha: ‘World-Honored One, since the Buddha attained perfect enlightenment fifty years ago, he has taught in various ways and given various instructions, transforming and saving sentient beings of every capacity. If there is a
supreme great Dharma
not yet taught, for me
(I pray, for me)

and for the bodhisattva practitioners of the final age, and for ordinary beings who wish to walk the Buddha’s path, set it forth and proclaim it.’ Having spoken these words, he gave up his body and made it a seat, adorned with heavenly garments, and had the Tathāgata sit upon it. Then the Tathāgata sat upon this jewel seat, received this lotus flower, and without speech or word simply held up the lotus flower before the eighty-four thousand humans and gods in the great assembly. At that time, the whole assembly fell silent. Then the elder Mahākāśyapa, seeing the Buddha hold up the flower and show it to the assembly as a Buddha-deed, was at once opened wide
(instantly greatly awakened)

, and broke into a smile. The Buddha then told him: ‘Just so. I have the treasury of the correct Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the subtle Dharma gate of true reality without marks, not established on words, a special transmission outside the teachings, the all-holding, all-sustaining, the becoming of Buddhas by ordinary beings, the ultimate truth — now I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.’”

[Buddha-deed: the teaching and transformation of the Buddhas is called a Buddha-deed. The Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: “In the Sahā world, one performs Buddha-deeds.” Kuoran: the appearance of all obstructions being removed, the sudden clearing of a blocked mind. Breaking into a smile: describing a heart that understands without words. Treasury of the correct Dharma eye: the Buddha’s mind-eye sees the correct Dharma thoroughly, and this is called the ‘correct Dharma eye’; it is deep and vast and contains all virtues, and that is called the ‘treasury.’ The wondrous mind of nirvāṇa:
the mind-substance of no-thought.

[Mind-substance of no-thought: the self-nature that dwells in the state of no-thought. When Patriarch Bodhidharma first transmitted it to the Second Patriarch Huike, it was precisely this mind-substance of no-thought.]
The Record of Pointing at the Moon says:
The Patriarch
(Patriarch Bodhidharma)

first dwelt at Shaolin Temple for nine years; when he taught the Dharma to the Second Patriarch, he only taught: ‘Externally put an end to all conditions; internally let the mind have no gasping; with the mind like a wall, one may enter the Way.’ Huike spoke of mind and nature in many ways
(Huike used various teachings to explain the mind-substance)
, and never once hit the mark; the Patriarch only rejected what was wrong in them
(Patriarch Bodhidharma merely negated his answers)
and did not explain for him
the mind-substance of no-thought
(did not plainly tell him that the answer is the mind-substance of no-thought)
. Huike suddenly said: ‘I have already put an end to all conditions
(I have already stilled all kinds of entanglement — that is, I am in the state of no-thought)
.’ The Patriarch said: ‘Have you not become annihilated?’ Huike said: ‘I have not become annihilated
(the numinous knowing is perfectly clear)
.’ The Patriarch said: ‘
This is the mind-substance transmitted by all the Buddhas
(this is the mind-substance of no-thought transmitted by all the Buddhas)
, doubt it no more.
[Externally put an end to all conditions: externally, still all kinds of entanglement. Internally let the mind have no gasping: internally, the mind does not give rise to thoughts.]
[True reality without marks: ‘true reality’ is the actual situation of all dharmas. The actual situation of all dharmas is that they simply do not exist — as the Sixth Patriarch said:
“Originally there is not a single thing.”
‘True reality without marks’ means: the actual situation of all dharmas is without marks. The Diamond Sūtra says:
“All that has marks is false and delusive.”
[Not established on words: ‘not established on words’ is spoken in contrast to
directly
“transmitting mind by mind.”
But because people take the words literally, they often mistakenly suppose that the Chan school does not use words.
In fact, are the texts, koans, and recorded sayings of the Chan school really so few?
Therefore the Chan patriarchs rebuked them, saying:
“Yet those who lose the meaning of ‘not established on words’
(who lose its original intent)
are many, and they often take the setting aside of words and silent sitting to be Chan — these are truly the dumb sheep of our house.”

[Special transmission outside the teachings: ‘the teachings’ refers to the scriptures. The Chan school’s direct transmission of the Buddha-patriarchs’ mind-seal is called ‘a special transmission outside the teachings,’ meaning a special transmission apart from the Tathāgata’s scriptures. Mind-seal: ‘mind’ is the Buddha-mind; ‘seal’ means to seal with approval or to seal and confirm. The Chan school does not establish words and does not rely on speech, but only transmits mind by mind, using the Buddha-mind to seal and confirm the minds of sentient beings and to realize the mark of non-duality.]

“Holding up a flower and smiling” — this was Śākyamuni Buddha’s mind-to-mind transmission, first transmitted to Mahākāśyapa, and so Mahākāśyapa is the first patriarch of the Chan school. Transmitted in order downward, Bodhidharma is the twenty-eighth patriarch, Huike the twenty-ninth, Sengcan the thirtieth, Daoxin the thirty-first, Hongren the thirty-second, and Huineng the thirty-third.

blocks.text: Sudden Enlightenment with Gradual Cultivation, and Gradual Cultivation with Sudden Enlightenment

inline.s: Question: What are sudden enlightenment with gradual cultivation and gradual cultivation with sudden enlightenment?
Answer: These are the two roads of practice, each with its own strength. Sudden enlightenment with gradual cultivation is, as the Formula for Cultivating the Mind says (see the Academy textbook
A Detailed Explanation of the Formula for Cultivating the Mind

), first to see one’s own nature, then to begin cultivation after awakening, tuning the mind and removing habitual tendencies, with samādhi and prajñā held equally. Gradual cultivation with sudden enlightenment takes awakening as its goal, investigating all the way to the end until one sees through to the original nature. Old Master Xuyun said: “Chan investigation must take awakening as its goal.” The awakening (seeing the nature) spoken of here is the falling away of faculties and objects and seeing through to the original nature. As the Compendium of the Five Lamps records, Chan Master Baizhang ascended the hall and said: “The numinous light shines alone, utterly free of faculties and objects. The substance reveals true constancy, not bound by words. Mind and nature are undefiled, originally perfect. Simply be free of deluded conditions (only do not recklessly entangle yourself with sense-objects), and you are thusness Buddha.”

Awakening has intellectual awakening and realized awakening. On this, Master Hanshan gave the instruction: “Among practitioners, there are those who awaken first and then cultivate, and those who cultivate first and then awaken; but awakening differs as intellectual and realized. To clarify the mind by relying on the words and teachings of the Buddhas and patriarchs is intellectual awakening: it mostly falls into views, and in all situations and conditions it is largely ineffective, because mind and objects stand opposed and cannot merge; wherever it goes it becomes stuck and creates many obstacles. This is called semblance prajñā, not true investigation. As for realized awakening, one works plainly and honestly from within one’s own mind, pressing on until the water runs out and the mountains end, when suddenly a single thought
(a subtle thought)

ceases at once, and one understands one’s own mind thoroughly, like seeing your own father at a crossroads — there is no further doubt. It is like one who drinks water, knowing for oneself whether it is cold or warm, and it cannot be spoken out to others. This is true investigation and genuine awakening. Then one uses the place of awakening to merge mind and objects, purifying away present karma and the flowing consciousness; deluded thoughts and emotional cares all melt into one flavor of true mind — this is realized awakening.” (Collected Works of Dream Wanderings·Reply to Vice Censor-in-Chief Zheng Kunyan)

With these two roads, sudden enlightenment with gradual cultivation and gradual cultivation with sudden enlightenment, whichever one you practice, you must attend to two points: first, do not mistake an illusion for the state of awakening; second, you must correctly judge the stage your practice has reached.

Whichever Dharma gate it is, the common route of practice is: subdue afflictions, cut off afflictions, attain the acceptance of non-arising, and perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. The superiority of the Chan school lies in cultivating from the ground of the nature, and so it is fierce, sharp, and swift; its route is: the ten thousand thoughts return to one, the one returns to nothing, see one’s own nature, subdue afflictions, cut off afflictions, attain the acceptance of non-arising, and perfectly realize the fruit of Buddhahood. The common Dharma gates must cut off afflictions before one can end birth and death and escape rebirth; whereas the Pure Land Dharma gate requires only that Buddha-recitation reach the point where the ten thousand thoughts return to one (single-minded concentration), and one can be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, ending birth and death and escaping rebirth — hence it is the easy path.

[Acceptance of non-arising: that is, the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas — true wisdom rests securely in the principle that ‘all dharmas were never born, and therefore also never cease,’ and no longer retrogresses.]

The Great Prajñā Sūtra says: “Thus the irreversible bodhisattva-mahāsattva, by the emptiness of own-marks, contemplates all dharmas and has already entered the bodhisattva’s right nature beyond birth, so that he does not see even the slightest dharma to be attained. Because nothing is attainable, there is nothing produced. Because nothing is produced, there is ultimately no arising. Because there is ultimately no arising, it is named the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. Because he obtains this acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, he is named an irreversible bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”

The acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is the bodhisattva’s personal realization of the ultimate emptiness of all dharmas; the bodhisattva obtains it when his practice reaches the seventh ground. The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom says: “Subhūti! The bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling
in the seventh ground
should not cling to twenty dharmas.
There are another twenty dharmas that should be brought to completion. What are the twenty? First, the perfection of emptiness; second, the realization of marklessness; …; ninth,
the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas

; …” [Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom: its full title is the Treatise Explaining the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra. One hundred fascicles, explaining the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra (also called the Great Prajñā Sūtra). Composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated by Kumārajīva.]

blocks.text: Subduing Afflictions and Cutting Off Afflictions

inline.s: Question: When the ten thousand thoughts return to one, one is able to subdue afflictions; when the one returns to nothing, there are no afflictions. Why does it say here that the sequence of study and practice is “the ten thousand thoughts return to one, the one returns to nothing, see one’s own nature, subdue afflictions, cut off afflictions”?

Answer: ‘The ten thousand thoughts return to one’ means being able to dwell stably in the state where only a single thought remains — but it does not require this all day long; ‘subduing afflictions,’ however, requires subduing afflictions so that they do not become active all day long — that is to say, if deluded thoughts arise, one never follows any of them (note especially the word ‘any’ in this sentence). ‘The one returns to nothing’ means being able to dwell stably in the state of no-thought — but it does not require this all day long; ‘cutting off afflictions,’ however, requires that there be no afflictions at all throughout the day — that is to say, both love and hate are extinguished.
Question: What are Tathāgata Chan and Patriarch Chan?

Answer: ‘Tathāgata Chan’ refers to the Chan methods prevalent in China before Bodhidharma came from the West, such as ānāpāna Chan, the five-gate Chan, and so on. Its characteristic is: cultivating contemplation in reliance on the teachings, gathering the mind and entering concentration, and advocating liberation through dhyāna. ‘Patriarch Chan’ refers to the Chan method transmitted by Patriarch Bodhidharma:
not established on words, a special transmission outside the teachings, pointing directly at the human mind, seeing the nature and becoming Buddha.

The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch says: “It discusses only seeing the nature; it does not discuss dhyāna and liberation.” The Sūtra of the Great Brahmā King’s Questions to the Buddha on Resolving Doubts says that the Brahmā King came to Vulture Peak, offered the Buddha a golden utpala flower, and asked the Buddha to teach the Dharma. The World-Honored One held up the flower and showed it to the assembly, and said nothing; at that moment the million humans and gods did not understand his meaning, and only the Venerable Kāśyapa was at once opened wide and broke into a smile. The World-Honored One said: “I have the treasury of the correct Dharma eye, the wondrous mind of nirvāṇa, the true reality without marks, the subtle Dharma gate, not established on words, a special transmission outside the teachings. I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa.” This is the origin of the Chan school. Therefore Patriarch Chan also originates from the Tathāgata — it is simply a special transmission outside the teachings.

[Pointing directly at the human mind: pointing directly at the fact that one’s own mind is Buddha, without seeking outside. The ‘mind’ here refers to the self-nature. The Essentials of Mind Transmission says:

“Only this one mind is Buddha; between Buddha and sentient beings there is no difference at all. But sentient beings cling to marks and seek outside; the more they seek, the more they lose it. They make Buddha seek Buddha, use mind to grasp mind, and though they exhaust kalpas and wear out their bodies, in the end they cannot attain it. They do not know that when thought ceases and cares are forgotten
(wang, that is, forgotten)

, the Buddha appears of himself. This mind is Buddha; Buddha is sentient beings. When one is a sentient being, this mind is not diminished; when one is a Buddha, this mind is not increased. Even the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices, and virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are originally complete in oneself and do not depend on cultivation to be added; when conditions come, it acts, and when conditions cease, it is still. If one is not firmly resolved and does not believe that this is Buddha, but wishes to cultivate with clinging to marks in order to seek merit and function, all of that is deluded thought and is contrary to the Way. This mind is Buddha; there is no other Buddha and no other mind. This mind is bright and pure, like empty space, with not the slightest mark. To raise the mind and stir a thought is to deviate from the Dharma-substance and to cling to marks; since beginningless time there has never been a Buddha who clings to marks. To cultivate the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices wishing to attain Buddhahood is to posit stages; since beginningless time there has never been a Buddha of stages.”

Seeing the nature and becoming Buddha: ‘seeing the nature and becoming Buddha’ means that through seeing one’s own nature, one cultivates from the ground of the nature and perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. Therefore, after seeing the nature one must still subdue afflictions, cut off afflictions, and attain the acceptance of non-arising, until at last one perfectly realizes the fruit of Buddhahood. Strictly speaking, only after seeing the nature does true cultivation begin; before seeing the nature, it can only be called preliminary practice. But because people take the words literally, they often mistakenly suppose that the Chan school holds that ‘seeing the nature is itself Buddhahood,’ and some even use this to attack the Chan school wildly. This is truly a misunderstanding of enormous proportions!]

It has already been said above that what Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted to the Second Patriarch was first awakening (personally realizing the mind-substance of no-thought) and then cultivating from the ground of the nature. In the Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch, in the section ‘Shenhui Pays His Respects’ of ‘Chapter Eight: Sudden and Gradual,’ it is recorded:
The Master
(the Sixth Patriarch)
also said: If your mind is deluded and you do not see, ask a good teacher to seek the road; if your mind is awakened, then see the nature for yourself and practice according to the Dharma.”

(The Sixth Patriarch instructed Shenhui: If you have not yet seen the nature, you should ask a good teacher to point out the road so that you may see the nature; if you have already seen the nature, you should practice according to the Dharma.) From this it can be seen that what the Sixth Patriarch transmitted was ‘first awakening (seeing the nature), and then cultivating from the ground of the nature.’ The Chan Grove Notes on the Jade Forest records:

In former days, Lan’an came to visit Chan Master Baizhang, bowed, and asked: “When a student wishes to come to know the Buddha, which is it?” Baizhang said: “That is much like riding an ox to seek an ox
(your own nature is Buddha — why speak of wishing to come to know the Buddha)
.” He said: “After knowing, what then
(after knowing the Buddha (seeing the nature), what should one do)
?” Baizhang said: “It is like a person riding an ox home
(causing the self-nature to return to its source)
.” He said: “I do not know how one should preserve and sustain it from beginning to end
(not knowing how, on the road home, one should preserve and sustain it from first to last)
?” Baizhang said: “Like a cowherd holding a staff and watching it, not letting it trample people’s sprouts and grain
(in the face of conditions and circumstances, cutting off habitual tendencies)

From this it can be known that what the First Patriarch of the Chan school, Bodhidharma, transmitted, what the Sixth Patriarch Huineng transmitted, and what the Sixth Patriarch’s descendant Chan Master Baizhang (the Sixth Patriarch transmitted to Huairang, Huairang to Mazu, Mazu to Baizhang) transmitted, is all ‘first awakening (seeing the nature), and then cultivating from the ground of the nature’
. How could it be that they advocated ‘seeing the nature is itself Buddhahood’?!

blocks.text: Investigating Apart from Mind, Intellect, and Consciousness

inline.s: Question: What does ‘investigating apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness’ mean?

Answer: Investigating apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness means investigating apart from thought. Gathering and arising is called mind; deliberating is called intellect; distinguishing is called consciousness. Among ‘mind, intellect, and consciousness,’ mind refers to the eighth consciousness (the ālaya consciousness), intellect refers to the seventh consciousness (the manas), and consciousness refers to the remaining six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness). ‘Investigating apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness’ means investigating while leaving behind the operations of the consciousness-mind (mind, intellect, and consciousness). (On the operations of the consciousness-mind, see in detail
Mind, Self-Nature, and Tathāgatagarbha
the section ‘The Working Process of the Consciousness-Mind.’) ‘Investigating apart from mind, intellect, and consciousness’ is also what the Sixth Patriarch said in the Platform Sūtra:
“I tell you students of the Way: in doing the work you must use the intellect; do not, having entered the Mahāyāna gate, still cling to the wisdom of birth and death.”

(Translation: I announce to all students of the Way that in doing the work one must use the intellect (the manas); do not, while studying the Mahāyāna Dharma gate, use the consciousness-mind to do the work.)

[Intellect: that is, the manas, also called the faculty of mind. The characteristic of the manas is constant and unremitting deliberation, giving rise to a discriminating mind. ‘In doing the work you must use the intellect’: the manas constantly deliberates and entangles itself with mental objects; the discriminating mind and deluded thoughts are often produced by it. Therefore Chan investigation is done with the manas: block the flow of deluded thoughts so that they cannot proceed, and right at the place where they cannot proceed, look into and behold your original face.]
Master Hanshan said:

“This above is the tongs and hammer that old man Dahui habitually used; its meaning is only to have you use the huatou to block the flow of deluded thoughts from the faculty of mind so that they cannot proceed, and right at the place where they cannot proceed, to look into and behold your original face. It is not teaching you to ponder over a koan, to take up doubt, or to seek an explanation.”
(Collected Works of Dream Wanderings
Essential Instructions on Chan Investigation)
[The wisdom of birth and death: the consciousness-mind.]
Question: How does one investigate with the intellect (the manas)?
Answer: For example, Patriarch Dahui said:
“Just set your mind to it, and think at the place where thinking cannot reach.”
Chan Master Yaoshan Weiyan said:
“Think the unthinkable.”
Chan Master Weishan Lingyou said:
“By the wonder of thinking the unthought, turn thought back upon the inexhaustible flame of the numinous.”
(See
The Chan Method of Dahui
Master Hanshan said:
“If you can truly apply the mind, apply effort solely at the point before a single thought arises.”
Collected Works of Dream Wanderings·Reply to the Monk Haiyin of Huzhou
) He also said:
“Simply, within each thought, watch the place where the thought has not yet arisen.”
(See
The One Move of Departing from Thought
Old Master Xuyun said:
“You must know that the true huatou is to be investigated at the point before a single thought has sprouted.”
(See
The Chan Method of Xuyun
When a deluded thought arises, at once see through it: a dream!
With the mind of awareness, dwell in the present moment: without judging, without struggling, without clinging.
What you do does not matter; what matters is doing it with presence.
Samādhi and prajñā held equally: be present, and be aware of that presence.
Take hold of the mind in each present moment.
Know that the mind moves deludedly and that no object lies before you; cultivate the Dharma of detachment, neither grasping nor thinking.
Totally accept the present moment (not grasping at marks) and connect with the inner (unmoving thusness).
Transformation will then occur (the forbearance of acquiescence, the forbearance of gentle compliance, and the acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas).

[No object before one: in fact there is no present object, because it is an illusion.] [Cultivating the Dharma of detachment: knowing the illusion, one is at once free of it; being free of the illusion, one is at once enlightened.]
Question: I have tried Dahui’s Chan method and Xuyun’s Chan method, and both felt extremely difficult. Is there a skillful means for investigating Chan?
Answer: The reason you find it difficult is that you do not yet possess the prerequisite for Chan investigation —
letting go of all conditions, and not a single thought arising

For Chan investigation is carried on in a stable state of no-thought; if the ten thousand conditions entangle you and thought after thought arises and ceases, can you still speak of investigating Chan? Therefore you should first do the work of ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one’ and ‘the one returns to nothing,’ so as to possess the prerequisite for Chan investigation — letting go of all conditions, and not a single thought arising.
If you have fairly good presence skill (see in detail, in the preliminary section of this book,
“Chapter Four: Awareness of the Present”

), then you can take the two words ‘be present’ as your huatou. Once this huatou is raised, you are at once in the state of presence, and so from the very start the huatou stands firm — this is the initial stage of ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one.’ Then you train how the huatou may stand steadily and stand long, gradually entering the state of ‘the one returns to nothing.’ Practiced in this way, it is relatively easy to let go of all conditions through ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one,’ and to reach ‘not a single thought arising’ through ‘the one returns to nothing,’ so as to possess the prerequisite for Chan investigation — letting go of all conditions, and not a single thought arising.
Question: Please explain what presence is.
Answer:
Presence is being aware of the present moment without giving rise to thoughts.

The chapters of the preliminary section are in fact ways of entering presence through different facets. Chapter One enters presence through awareness of movement; Chapter Two through awareness of feeling; Chapter Three through awareness of the breath; Chapter Four through awareness of scenes, sounds, the self-nature, the present moment, and so on; Chapter Five through awareness of thoughts. Therefore, through the study and practice of the preliminary section, you already possess considerable capacity for presence, and to investigate Awareness Chan at this point is like water arriving and the channel forming of itself. Presence is the foundation of investigating Awareness Chan. So you must train your presence skill solidly (see in detail this book’s
“Chapter Four: Awareness of the Present”
). When presence skill is solid, so that you are present at all times while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, the cultivation that follows will go smoothly.
Question: Is presence dhyāna (meditative concentration)?
Answer: The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“What is called dhyāna and concentration? To be outwardly free of marks is dhyāna; to be inwardly undisturbed is concentration.”

That is to say, inwardly not turning with thoughts and outwardly not pulled by objects — this is dhyāna and concentration. So presence is dhyāna and concentration; this is the dhyāna and concentration of the Chan lineage (different from the four dhyānas and eight concentrations of the doctrinal schools).

[Chan lineage: the Chan school’s name for itself. Other schools, such as the Tiantai school, the Pure Land school, and the Faxiang school, are all called doctrinal schools.] [Four dhyānas and eight concentrations: the four dhyānas are the four meditative concentrations of the form realm; the four meditative concentrations of the form realm together with the four formless concentrations of the formless realm are called the eight concentrations.]
Presence is concentration; being aware of that presence is prajñā. To hold concentration and prajñā equally, to cultivate both — this is correct.

[Being aware of that presence: presence has three levels, from shallow to deep. First, be aware of the things around you; second, feel the life-force (energy field) within the body; third, be aware of that presence. When you first practice, you may enter level by level. Once familiar, you enter directly.]

The study and practice of Awareness Chan has four stages: first, the ten thousand thoughts return to one; second, the one returns to nothing; third, earnest investigation; fourth, breaking through the three barriers. Within these four stages, it is through earnest investigation that one breaks through the three barriers. And the prerequisite for investigation (looking back at one’s own original face) is: letting go of all conditions, and not a single thought arising. Otherwise, with the ten thousand conditions entangling you and thought after thought arising and ceasing, how can you look back at your own original face? Therefore you must first, through the work of ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one,’ let go of all conditions, and then, through ‘the one returns to nothing,’ reach ‘not a single thought arising.’ At that point, having possessed the prerequisite for Chan investigation, ‘letting go of all conditions, and not a single thought arising,’ you enter the stage of ‘earnest investigation’ in order to break through the three barriers.

The essence of athletic training — ‘three froms and one great’: from difficulty, from strictness, from actual combat, and a great volume of training — is entirely suited to investigating Awareness Chan as well: from difficulty (practicing only in the ‘learning zone’), from strictness (not tolerating the slightest slackness), from actual combat (polishing yourself amid conditions and circumstances), and a great volume of training (throughout all the hours of the day, never setting the work aside whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down).

blocks.text: Chapter One: The Ten Thousand Thoughts Return to One

inline.s: The method for doing the work of ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one’ is: raise the phrase ‘be present,’ and you at once enter the state of presence — aware without thought or thinking, and clearly knowing for yourself that there is no thought or thinking. ‘Clearly knowing for yourself that there is no thought or thinking’ — this point is extremely important; otherwise it is concentration without prajñā. The essential point of Awareness Chan is to hold concentration and prajñā equally. The Treatise on Cutting Off Contemplation says:
“The mind-nature being still and extinguished is concentration; constantly understanding stillness and extinction is prajñā.”
[Raising the phrase ‘be present’: there are usually three ways of reciting it — aloud, silently, and vajra recitation. Vajra recitation is moving the lips and tongue without making a sound.]
The essential points of presence are: alertness, awareness, and non-judgment.
Dwell with the mind of awareness: let the three hundred and sixty joints and the eighty-four thousand pores of the whole body be aware of the present moment, keeping up the vigilance day and night.
Master Hanshan wrote in verse:
“If wherever you touch you turn the light back to shine, the dust of toil will not entrap the master within.”
(Collected Works of Dream Wanderings) The Sixth Patriarch said:

“If you wish to know the essentials of the mind, simply do not think about anything good or evil, and you will naturally enter the pure mind-substance, serene and ever still, with wondrous function as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.”
(The Platform Sūtra of the Sixth Patriarch)

[Keeping up vigilance: alertly maintaining right mindfulness. Master Lianchi said: “I pray that you let go of all conditions and, throughout the twelve hours (twenty-four hours), keep up mindfulness in every thought — this is my earnest hope.” (Collected Works of Yunqi) The Complete Works of Master Zhu, ‘Preserving and Nurturing,’ says: “Simply keep up vigilance always; accumulating little by little, in time it will naturally continue without break and become one piece.” For example, the monk Ruiyan would often ask himself each day: “Master, are you clear and awake?” and would answer himself: “Clear and awake.”]
[Clear and awake: clear-minded. For a practitioner, falling into deluded thought or into torpor is to be unclear-minded, because one is not in charge of oneself.]
[Dust of toil: the mind toiling over sense-objects; another name for affliction.] [Master: the master within, meaning the self-nature.]

The instruction ‘be present’ is the huatou, and the state of presence (aware without thought or thinking) is itself the doubt-mass. If the doubt-mass is present, there is no need to raise the huatou again; if the doubt-mass is absent (deluded thought or torpor), you must raise it at once. Because of the study and practice of the preliminary section, to attain ‘raise the phrase “be present,” and at once enter the state of presence’ is quite easy — in fact, from the very start of Chan investigation you step into the stage where ‘the huatou stands firm.’

The problem now is this: to keep the huatou from being lost, and to make the doubt-mass (the state of presence) continuous, lasting, and resistant to interference. This can only be achieved through repeated training. So do not forget to raise the huatou whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down; and as soon as the huatou is raised, you must be present — never allow deluded thoughts to run on into a train of thinking. You must attain this: the moment the huatou is raised, deluded thoughts vanish completely. Remind yourself at all times: free yourself from the control of the head (of thought) and be present.
On the
One-Minute Meditation

web page there is an audio player: after one minute, a bell sounds. (Right-click the play button; you can set the playlist to repeat in the menu, or download it.) You can use it to measure how long you can keep aware and thought-free after raising a huatou, and use it as a tool to help you practice gradually lengthening that time. This is a most important basic skill; you must work hard and train it well.

One who investigates Awareness Chan should, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, never forget ‘presence’; even if sleepiness comes, as soon as one is aware, continue. Do not let other matters interrupt it, do not let greed, anger, and delusion come between, and repent as soon as a fault is committed. Never apart from it in any thought — present in every thought.
When the work is deep, you no longer need to raise the huatou; you can dwell in presence freely and for long periods, and enter the state of ‘the one thought returns to nothing.’
Question: Letting go of all conditions is actually quite difficult to do. What method should be used to deal with this?
Answer: The way to deal with it is: use principle to remove the thing, and use the huatou to resist. Whenever you meet a situation or condition you cannot let go of, at once realize:
“All that has marks is false and delusive”
, and
believe in your own nature
(believe that your own nature is originally Buddha)
, know that the mind moves deludedly and that no object lies before you
(when an object appears before you, know that this is your own mind moving deludedly, and that in fact there is no present object)
, and cultivate the Dharma of detachment

. If you have thought the principle through but still cannot let go, then resist with the huatou. So when the principle has been thought through and you still cannot let go, this is the doing of karmic forces and habitual tendencies; at such a time, raise the huatou with great fierce courage, and you will be able to let go.
The sages of old taught, saying:
If the mind runs astray, resist it with the huatou, and in time it will grow still of itself.
In learning any Dharma, who does not use bitter effort? If one did not apply effort, and could suddenly
jù
, at once)
let go — why would one need to study?”

Question: I am a Buddha-recitation practitioner. I use the Buddha’s name in place of the words ‘be present’: I raise the Buddha’s name and at once enter the state of presence. Is it all right to do this?
Answer: Entirely all right.
Question: Sometimes a hateful thought circles around and will not leave, and it becomes unbearable. Though I keep telling myself not to think about it anymore, it has no effect. What should I do?

Answer: This is like being shrouded in darkness: the most effective thing is to find the light switch. Press the switch, and the darkness is driven away. The switch that drives out deluded thought is awareness. When you are in the situation where a thought circles and will not leave, what you need to do is to say aloud: “Be present!” At once raise awareness, enter presence, and the deluded thought ceases of itself. In fact, deluded thoughts are like a sparring partner — they give you a place to use your skill. Always observe whether you are caught in deluded thinking; play this game like hide-and-seek. As soon as you notice you are lost in deluded thinking, at once say: “Be present!” Raise awareness, enter presence, and the deluded thinking ceases of itself. Practice this long, and the work of ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one’ is accomplished.

Once upon a time, a monk went alone into the deep mountains to practice. When night came, he saw a fierce ghost rush at him. In his peril he hurriedly recited the Buddha’s name, and the fierce ghost retreated again and again. But as soon as the recitation stopped, the ghost pressed forward again, so he had to recite without stopping the whole night through. Only at daybreak did the ghost leave. The same happened for several nights afterward. So the monk simply slept during the day and recited the Buddha’s name all night long. Thus he held out year after year. In the end he attained the Buddha-recitation samādhi, and the fierce ghost vanished without a trace. He was deeply, deeply grateful to that fierce ghost.

In fact, every Chan practitioner also faces a fierce ghost — deluded thought. It watches day and night, wanting to devour our Dharma-body and wisdom-life. So you must stay highly alert and use the huatou to beat back its every attack in time. The outcome is plain: either you defeat it and accomplish your work on the path, or it defeats you and leaves you still turning in birth and death.
Question: It was said above that one should ‘say: “Be present!” and at once raise awareness, enter presence, and the deluded thinking ceases of itself.’ Aware of what?

Answer: Be aware of the object you find most convenient and most effective: movement, feeling, the breath, scenes, sounds, the self-nature, or thoughts — any of them will do. For example, if in studying the preliminary section you put the greatest effort into awareness of movement, and awareness of movement is most effective for you in stilling deluded thoughts, then at once be aware of movement and enter presence.
Question: But at the time I am motionless, lying in bed — what then?

Answer: You can create movement. For example, the finger-twirling method: with the thumb slowly and repeatedly rub (stroke) the middle finger and the index finger, attentively aware of each movement and of the sensation of contact between the fingers, with the mind following the fingers. Once you are familiar with this practice, body and mind enter with ease a state of serene peace that is yet aware.

There are two situations in practice: training and actual combat. Training means deliberately assigning yourself training exercises and preparing for actual combat. Actual combat means that when you meet situations and conditions, you must still deluded thoughts and concentrate the mind on one point. (Since this is the stage of ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one,’ the requirement in actual combat is to still deluded thoughts; in the stage of ‘the one returns to nothing,’ the requirement in actual combat is no-thought.) Actual combat is both the basis for designing training exercises and the test of training’s effectiveness, and indeed its very purpose. You are your own coach; you must train yourself systematically, scientifically, and solidly.

When deluded thinking circles and will not leave, you can also deal with it this way: silently repeat “Thought —, thought —, …” Each time you say “Thought —,” attentively look at the thought in your mind and see what it is; then say “Thought —” again, and attentively look at the thought in your mind and see what it is. Continue in this way until the deluded thinking ceases.

Remember: the harder the time and place for doing the work, the more you must do it there — these are the best times for advancing your practice. A strong opponent is your best coach; that is why in chess one seeks out a master to play. Your one goal is to defeat it!
When Śākyamuni Buddha, beneath the bodhi tree, saw the morning star at night and awakened to the Way, he said:
“How wonderful! How wonderful! All sentient beings possess the Tathāgata’s wisdom and virtue-marks in full, but because of deluded thinking and attachment they cannot realize them.

And deluded thinking and attachment are concentrated above all in thoughts. Therefore, though there are many roads of practice, everything comes down to working on the thought — to catch a bandit, first catch the chief. So practice is simple too: it is nothing but a thought! As long as you keep your eye on this thought at all times and in all places and are not toyed with by it, there is no practice that cannot succeed.
Question: I am often shrouded in negative emotions. What should I do?

Answer: You have now attained ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one’ and can dwell in presence continuously. This is like a poor child who has become a rich man — you should no longer live a life of hardship. So you must learn to spend your money. How? In the book
Practicing the Power of Now

by Eckhart Tolle, many concrete methods are explained; you can read while you practice and practice while you read. What is wonderful is that the more of your ‘money’ you spend, the more suffering you are spared — and your wealth not only does not decrease, it grows by leaps and bounds.

‘Looking back at that thinker’ is an effective way to still deluded thinking. You can do it anytime and anywhere, and this too is doing the work of no-thought. Being without thought, you will not be shrouded in negative emotions, and you will find inner stillness, peace, and joy.
The Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“All sentient beings, from beginningless time, have had all kinds of inversion, like a confused person who mistakes the four directions
(for example, taking east for west and south for north, and so on)

, falsely taking the four great elements as the mark of their own body and the shadows of the six sense-objects as the mark of their own mind. It is like a person with a diseased eye who sees flowers in the sky and a second moon. Good sons! The sky truly has no flowers; the sick person falsely clings to them. Because of this false clinging, they are not only confused about the nature of this emptiness, but also deluded about where the real flowers arise. From this false existence they turn around in birth and death; therefore it is called ignorance.”

The shadows of the six sense-objects are the various thoughts and imaginings produced when the six faculties come into contact with the six sense-objects, and since these thoughts and imaginings are all illusory and unreal, they are called the shadows of the six sense-objects — the phantom shadows produced when the six faculties come into contact with the six sense-objects. Therefore, thought is not you! Remember this firmly. As long as you attentively look back at that thinker, thought cannot shroud you or control you, and you abide in the state of awareness.
Of course, turning the hearing back to the hearing-nature is also an effective way to still deluded thinking. You can do it anytime and anywhere, and this too is doing the work of no-thought.
Question: How does one turn the hearing back to the hearing-nature?
Answer: On this, the Formula for Cultivating the Mind has a most brilliant instruction:

“Moreover, the ways of entering the principle are many; I point out one gate for you, to make you return to the source. Do you still hear the cawing of crows and the chirping of magpies? He said: I hear. He said: Turn back and hear your hearing-nature. Are there still many sounds? He said: At this point all sounds and all discriminations are utterly unattainable. He said: How wonderful! How wonderful! This is the gate by which Guanyin entered the principle. Let me ask you further: you say, ‘At this point all sounds and all discriminations are altogether unattainable’ — since they are unattainable, at such a moment is it not empty space? He said: It is originally not empty; it is clear and not obscured. He said: What is the substance that is not empty? He said: It has no marks either; words cannot reach it. He said: This is the lifespan of all Buddhas and patriarchs; doubt it no more.”
Question: In ‘A Letter Discussing Chan’ in Chapter Two, Old Master Xuyun said:
“The true huatou is to be investigated at the point before a single thought has sprouted.”
I like this Chan method very much, but it is extremely difficult to do. Is there a skillful means?

Answer: Then you need to find a point of entry. You may try the following route. First, practice according to the method of ‘the ten thousand thoughts return to one’ as described above. When that work is mature, do the work of ‘be present, and then be aware of that presence.’ When you are familiar with this work, gradually begin to ‘investigate at the point before a single thought has sprouted.’ First do the work in stillness, then gradually extend it into movement. Do not be anxious for quick results; take each step solidly, and keep a long-range mind.

Presence (concentration), and being aware of that presence (prajñā). This is the easiest way to hold concentration and prajñā equally, and the easiest way for the mind-substance to be free of thought. The Awakening of Faith says:

“The mind-substance is free of thought; the mark of being free of thought is equal to the realm of empty space and pervades everywhere. The dharma realm’s one mark is the Tathāgata’s equal dharmakāya; in dependence on this dharmakāya it is named original enlightenment.”
